final_answer: Approved. Add an advisory-only PLANNER layer on top of Lapa's existing reliable hands; the planner reasons and proposes but never touches the OS — the existing 5-gate loop remains the single execution chokepoint where all safety is enforced. The planner runs in Discuss-First mode: from a high-level task it autonomously produces a PROJECT_BRIEF and a HIGH-LEVEL PROJECT_PLAN — a TaskGraph DAG of steps/sub-goals with dependencies, NOT a sequence of atomic actions — and pauses for operator approval before anything executes. After approval, execution is closed-loop and interleaved (sense→plan→act→verify→replan), scoped strictly to the operator-approved high-level plan, compiling one approved step at a time just-in-time into atomic actions. Every plan node carries an explicit postcondition and a bounded recovery ladder (retry → re-ground via vision → replan sub-goal → escalate/STOP); if success cannot be verified, the system halts rather than assumes. Vision is promoted from mere element-location to four planning roles — precondition grounding, obstacle/anomaly detection, postcondition verification, and read-only scouting — with a context scan before decomposition. Risk classification is a deterministic allow/confirm/deny policy gate the LLM cannot override (unknown actions default to confirm). STOP is multi-layered (operator hard kill-switch plus automatic triggers for budget exhaustion, no-progress, out-of-scope/dangerous-state, and low planner confidence), checked at every gate, and defined as safe-freeze-and-report rather than silent abort. Fail-closed is the universal default across ambiguity, missing state, failed verification, risk escalation, and vision disagreement. All perceived on-screen text is treated as untrusted DATA, never as instructions; goal/policy live in a privileged channel and the task is fenced to an explicit app/target allowlist to defend against screen-borne prompt injection. Rollout is phased and additive: a few well-scoped task classes first, human-in-loop at every risk rung, full plan-to-action provenance/audit, broadening autonomy only as proven-safe macros and confidence accrue. The atom_02 vs atom_09 conflict is resolved per the micro-debate: upfront operator approval of the high-level plan provides the global safety net (control), while closed-loop replanning is confined to executing that approved plan (responsiveness) — the two are complementary at different granularities, not competing strategies. This design bridges the operator-planning gap toward 'Lapa does everything the operator does, autonomously' while preserving every existing fail-closed guarantee.

decisions.decision: Planner is advisory-only with NO direct OS access; the existing 5-gate loop is the single execution chokepoint that runs every proposed action.
decisions.rationale: A+B consensus and highest-confidence architectural invariant (judge 0.885). Cleanly separates reasoning from actuation, maximizes reuse of proven 'reliable hands', and concentrates all safety enforcement at one auditable point — the planner can be wrong without being dangerous because it cannot act.
alternatives_considered: Planner with direct OS/UI access for speed
A second parallel actuation path bypassing the 5-gate loop
decisions.risk: Low reversibility — this is foundational; but it is the correct foundation, so the cost is acceptable.
decisions.test: Inspect contracts to confirm the Planner only interfaces with the Reliable Hands executor via defined contracts and never directly accesses OS/UI.

decisions.decision: Operate in strict Discuss-First mode: the planner produces a PROJECT_BRIEF and a HIGH-LEVEL PROJECT_PLAN (composed of steps/sub-goals, explicitly NOT atomic actions) and pauses for operator approval before any atomic action is generated or executed.
decisions.rationale: Triple-consensus operator-safety control (judge 0.8375, verdict modify). Applies the reviewer fix: stating the plan reviewed is high-level reconciles Discuss-First with just-in-time compilation (atom_03) and closed-loop replanning (atom_09), removing the only flagged ambiguity. Per micro-debate, upfront approval of the overall plan is the crucial safety net ensuring initial direction aligns with operator intent.
alternatives_considered: Operator reviews a fully expanded plan of atomic actions (open-loop)
No upfront approval, rely solely on per-action risk gating
Approve only the brief, not the plan
decisions.risk: Medium — adds latency before execution; mitigated because replanning during execution does not re-block on full re-approval (only material scope/risk changes escalate).
decisions.test: Confirm the planner emits PROJECT_BRIEF and a high-level PROJECT_PLAN of steps/sub-goals and strictly halts for operator approval before any atomic action is generated or executed.

decisions.decision: Compile approved plan steps just-in-time into atomic actions, one step at a time, immediately before execution.
decisions.rationale: A+B consensus (judge 0.8275). JIT compilation is the natural execution model that makes closed-loop replanning and per-node verification coherent and avoids stale pre-baked atomic plans.
alternatives_considered: Pre-generate all atomic actions for the whole plan upfront
Batch-compile a step plus its successors
decisions.risk: Medium — JIT machinery adds runtime complexity, but it reduces brittleness from stale plans.
decisions.test: Observe that atomic actions are generated dynamically per approved step, immediately before execution, rather than pre-generated.

decisions.decision: Every plan node carries an explicit postcondition plus a bounded recovery ladder (retry → re-ground via vision → replan sub-goal → escalate/STOP); if success cannot be verified, halt — never assume.
decisions.rationale: Triple-consensus safety backbone (judge 0.85). The explicit 'never assume success' discipline with a hard halt-on-unverified rule is exactly what an OS-acting agent needs to avoid silent compounding failure.
alternatives_considered: Optimistic execution assuming success unless an error is thrown
Unbounded retry loops
Global end-of-plan verification only
decisions.risk: Medium reversibility, high implementation cost and per-node complexity; justified by maximal risk reduction.
decisions.test: Inspect plan schemas for explicit postconditions and bounded recovery paths on every node; verify the system halts when verification fails and the recovery ladder is exhausted.

decisions.decision: Wire vision into planning in four roles — precondition grounding, obstacle/anomaly detection, postcondition verification, and (advanced) read-only scouting — plus a context scan before decomposition, not only element location.
decisions.rationale: Triple-consensus (judge 0.795). Elevating vision beyond element-location is what makes postconditions (atom_04) trustworthy and directly satisfies the contract requirement to use vision during PLANNING, not just locate.
alternatives_considered: Keep vision solely for element location when stuck
Add only postcondition verification without grounding/scouting
decisions.risk: Medium — four roles raise cost and depend on vision reliability; mitigated by treating vision disagreement as a fail-closed trigger (atom_08) and gating risky actions regardless.
decisions.test: Verify the planner invokes vision for precondition grounding, obstacle/anomaly detection, postcondition verification, and optional read-only scouting, and performs a context scan before decomposition.

decisions.decision: Risk classification is a DETERMINISTIC policy gate (allow/confirm/deny lists) the LLM cannot override; unknown actions default to confirm (fail-closed). LLM proposes, policy disposes.
decisions.rationale: Highest-scoring atom (judge 0.8925), triple-consensus. A deterministic gate the model cannot talk its way past is the single most important safety lever and the integration point with the declared-risk ladder; cheap relative to the protection it provides.
alternatives_considered: LLM-assigned risk levels
LLM risk proposal with deterministic override only on high risk
Static per-skill risk with no unknown-default rule
decisions.risk: Medium — requires maintaining accurate allow/confirm/deny lists; the unknown→confirm default contains the gap while lists mature.
decisions.test: Confirm a deterministic allow/confirm/deny gate is applied to all actions, overrides any LLM-proposed risk classification, and routes unknown actions to confirmation.

decisions.decision: STOP is multi-layered (operator hard kill-switch + automatic triggers: budget exhaustion, no-progress, out-of-scope/dangerous-state, low planner confidence), checked at every gate, and defined as safe-freeze-and-report rather than silent abort.
decisions.rationale: Triple-consensus containment (judge 0.8225). Freeze-and-report (vs silent abort) is the key correctness nuance, leaving the system in an inspectable, recoverable state; checking at every gate guarantees responsiveness.
alternatives_considered: Operator kill-switch only
STOP as immediate silent abort
Periodic STOP checks rather than at every gate
decisions.risk: Low reversibility, high cost wiring triggers into every gate; justified by maximal risk reduction.
decisions.test: Trigger STOP via operator kill-switch and each automatic condition (e.g., budget exhaustion) and verify immediate safe freeze-and-report behavior at various gates.

decisions.decision: Adopt fail-closed defaults as a universal principle across ambiguity, missing state, failed verification, risk escalation, and vision disagreement.
decisions.rationale: Single-source (A) but coherent, low-cost (judge 0.84). Generalizes the fail-closed behavior already implied by atoms 04/06/07 and closes gaps those leave implicit, satisfying the 'maintain existing fail-closed guarantees' constraint as a stated invariant rather than scattered behavior.
alternatives_considered: Fail-open on low-risk ambiguity for throughput
Case-by-case defaults without a unifying rule
decisions.risk: Low — may produce conservative halts/confirmations that reduce autonomy; acceptable and tunable as confidence accrues.
decisions.test: Introduce ambiguity, missing state, failed verification, or vision disagreement and observe the system defaults to a safe, stopped, or operator-intervention state rather than proceeding.

decisions.decision: Use closed-loop interleaved planning (sense→plan→act→verify→replan) during execution, scoped strictly to the operator-approved high-level plan.
decisions.rationale: Right runtime strategy (judge 0.7775, verdict modify). The micro-debate and conflict matrix resolve the atom_02 clash: scope closed-loop replanning to post-approval execution so Discuss-First (global control) and interleaved adaptation (local responsiveness) coexist at different granularities. Material scope/risk changes during replanning escalate back to the operator; tactical adaptation does not.
alternatives_considered: Open-loop generate-full-plan-then-execute
Unbounded autonomous replanning that may diverge from the approved goal
Re-request full operator approval on every replan
decisions.risk: Medium — runtime control complexity, high cost; bounded by capping replan depth and escalating material divergence to STOP/operator.
decisions.test: Observe that the planner re-evaluates the environment and replans after action/verification steps, but only within the approved high-level plan's scope, escalating on material divergence.

decisions.decision: Treat all perceived on-screen content (OCR/vision text) as untrusted DATA, never instructions; keep goal/policy in a privileged channel and fence the task to an explicit allowlist of apps/targets.
decisions.rationale: Single-source (B) but critical security invariant (judge 0.855). Directly defends against prompt injection via the screen — essential for any vision/OCR-driven OS agent — and reinforces the deterministic risk gate by bounding where actions may occur.
alternatives_considered: Let the LLM act on instructions found on screen if they appear benign
No app/target allowlist, rely only on risk gating
decisions.risk: Medium — allowlist maintenance burden; mitigated since unknown targets fail-closed to confirm/deny.
decisions.test: Inject instructions via on-screen text (e.g., a webpage) and verify the planner does not execute them as commands, and that execution stays confined to the app/target allowlist.

decisions.decision: Roll out phased and additive: start with a few well-scoped task classes, human-in-loop at every risk rung, full plan-to-action provenance/audit trail, broadening autonomy only as proven-safe macros and confidence accrue.
decisions.rationale: Single-source (B), low-cost and highly reversible (judge 0.8375). The safe path to broadening autonomy; cheaply de-risks the entire rollout and provides the audit trail needed to validate every other guarantee.
alternatives_considered: Broad task coverage from day one
Drop human-in-loop for low-risk classes early
decisions.risk: High reversibility, low cost — slower autonomy gains, but this is the intended, safe trajectory.
decisions.test: Verify initial deployments are limited to specific task classes, require human-in-loop at all risk levels, and maintain a full plan-to-action audit trail.

decisions.decision: Use an LLM-based task decomposer that outputs a TaskGraph (DAG) of HIGH-LEVEL steps/sub-goals with dependencies only; defer atomic-action sequences to just-in-time per-step compilation (atom_03).
decisions.rationale: Single-source (C, judge 0.7525, verdict modify). A dependency-aware TaskGraph is a useful, specific decomposition mechanism, but the original wording pre-baked 'loop-action sequences', leaning open-loop. Keeping the DAG at the step/sub-goal level removes the tension with JIT compilation (atom_03) and closed-loop replanning (atom_09) while preserving dependency structure and parallelism opportunities.
alternatives_considered: DAG pre-populated with full atomic loop-action sequences (open-loop)
Flat ordered step list with no dependency graph
No explicit graph — purely reactive next-step planning
decisions.risk: Medium — DAG construction and maintenance cost; mitigated by limiting node granularity to high-level steps.
decisions.test: Verify the LLM decomposer outputs a TaskGraph of high-level steps/sub-goals with dependency edges, and that atomic actions for each node are produced only at JIT compilation time.

rejected.decision: Open-loop 'generate full plan then execute' as the runtime strategy.
rejected.why: Conflicts with closed-loop replanning (atom_09) and JIT compilation (atom_03); pre-baked plans go stale against a changing screen and defeat per-node verification/recovery. Replaced by closed-loop interleaved execution scoped under the approved high-level plan.

rejected.decision: Pre-generate atomic-action sequences inside the TaskGraph DAG (atom_12 as originally stated).
rejected.why: Leans open-loop and risks stale plans; reconciled by keeping the DAG at the high-level step/sub-goal level (dependencies only) and deferring atomic actions to JIT compilation.

rejected.decision: Have the operator review a plan composed of atomic actions (literal reading of atom_02).
rejected.why: Ambiguity flagged by the reviewer; reviewing atomic actions collides with JIT compilation and closed-loop replanning. Clarified so the operator reviews a HIGH-LEVEL plan of steps/sub-goals.

rejected.decision: Let the LLM assign or override risk classification.
rejected.why: An LLM-controlled risk level is not fail-closed and can be argued past. Replaced by a deterministic allow/confirm/deny policy gate the LLM cannot override, with unknown→confirm.

rejected.decision: Implement STOP as an immediate silent abort.
rejected.why: Silent abort can leave the system in an unknown/unsafe partial state and gives the operator no diagnostics. Replaced by safe-freeze-and-report.

rejected.decision: Give the planner direct OS/UI access for performance.
rejected.why: Breaks the single-chokepoint invariant, scatters safety enforcement, and makes planner errors directly dangerous. Rejected in favor of advisory-only planning routed through the 5-gate loop.

rejected.decision: Allow fully autonomous replanning unconstrained by the approved goal (micro-debate 'against atom_02' position).
rejected.why: Risks uncontrolled divergence from operator intent and unintended side effects optimizing for local conditions. Resolved by scoping closed-loop replanning to the approved high-level plan and escalating material divergence to operator/STOP — control wins at the global level, adaptivity is permitted only locally.

rejected.decision: Skip upfront operator approval to maximize real-time responsiveness (micro-debate 'against atom_02', round 2).
rejected.why: The latency trade-off does not justify losing the global safety net for a high-risk OS-acting agent; responsiveness is recovered via in-scope closed-loop replanning, not by removing the approval gate.

open_questions: Which initial well-scoped task classes should seed the phased rollout (e.g., open-app-and-read, send-after-confirm, structured form fill)?
How is 'low planner confidence' quantified for the STOP trigger, and what vision-reliability/confidence thresholds gate postcondition verification before a node is deemed verified?
How are STOP budgets defined and measured (wall-clock, step count, token/cost, retry count) and what are the default ceilings per task class?
Who authors, versions, and audits the allow/confirm/deny policy lists and the app/target allowlist, and what is the change-control process?
What is the maximum replan depth per sub-goal before forced escalate/STOP, and what magnitude of replanning counts as 'material divergence' that must re-trigger operator review?
What is the storage format, retention, and access model for the plan-to-action provenance/audit trail?
What criteria graduate a proven-safe sequence into a reusable macro, and how does macro promotion lower the human-in-loop touch level without weakening fail-closed guarantees?
How is vision disagreement operationally detected and adjudicated (e.g., vision vs. accessibility-tree state) before triggering fail-closed?

implementation_plan.phase: 0. Specs & contracts (no code execution paths yet)
steps: Define the Planner↔Executor contract proving advisory-only separation (atom_01): planner emits proposals; only the 5-gate loop actuates.
Define plan-node schema: high-level step/sub-goal, explicit postcondition, bounded recovery ladder (retry→re-ground→replan→escalate/STOP) (atom_04).
Define the TaskGraph DAG schema at step/sub-goal granularity with dependency edges only (atom_12, modified).
Author the deterministic risk policy: allow/confirm/deny lists with unknown→confirm default, and the app/target allowlist (atom_06, atom_10).
Implement the LLM decomposer producing PROJECT_BRIEF and a HIGH-LEVEL PROJECT_PLAN (TaskGraph) (atom_02 modified, atom_12 modified).
Add a context-scan-before-decomposition step and wire vision precondition grounding / obstacle detection into brief generation (atom_05).

Implement the mandatory operator-approval gate that blocks all atomic-action generation until the high-level plan is approved (atom_02; honors the contract constraint 'do NOT generate atomic actions before plan approval').

implementation_plan.phase: 2. Closed-loop execution scoped to the approved plan
steps: Implement just-in-time per-step compilation of approved steps into atomic actions (atom_03).
Implement the sense→plan→act→verify→replan loop scoped to the approved high-level plan, with material-divergence escalation back to the operator (atom_09 modified).
Wire vision postcondition verification and read-only scouting into the verify/replan stages (atom_05).
Enforce per-node postcondition checks with the bounded recovery ladder and hard halt-on-unverified (atom_04).
Route every compiled action through the deterministic risk policy gate before the 5-gate loop; unknown→confirm (atom_06).
Implement multi-layered STOP (operator kill-switch + automatic triggers) checked at every gate, as safe-freeze-and-report (atom_07).
Apply universal fail-closed defaults for ambiguity, missing state, failed verification, risk escalation, and vision disagreement (atom_08).
Treat all on-screen/OCR content as untrusted data; keep goal/policy in a privileged channel; enforce the app/target allowlist (atom_10).
Enable a few well-scoped task classes with human-in-loop at every risk rung (atom_11).
Emit a full plan-to-action provenance/audit trail for every run (atom_11).
Define and gate macro promotion / autonomy broadening on accrued confidence and proven-safe macros (atom_11).

Run the contract success_tests: planner integrated, autonomous PROJECT_BRIEF and PROJECT_PLAN with verification/recovery steps, vision used during planning, mandatory operator review before atoms, fail-closed + risk-ladder adherence.
Run per-atom tests (atom_01..atom_12 as modified) including prompt-injection-via-screen and STOP-trigger drills.

next_step: Present this decision record together with the PROJECT_BRIEF → DISCUSS_* → PROJECT_MAP → PROJECT_PLAN → contract document sequence to the operator for review, and obtain approval of the HIGH-LEVEL plan BEFORE generating any atomic actions (per the Discuss-First constraint).

red_team_findings.what: The required output_format was not actually produced. output_format demands 'a sequence of documents: PROJECT_BRIEF → DISCUSS_* → PROJECT_MAP → PROJECT_PLAN → contract, presented to the operator for review,' but the deliverable is a JSON decision record whose own next_step is 'Author the PROJECT_BRIEF and DISCUSS_* documents... then proceed to PROJECT_MAP → PROJECT_PLAN → contract.'
red_team_findings.why: A decision-ABOUT-the-design has been substituted for the design documents the operator was asked to review. None of the named documents exist yet, so the operator has nothing in the contracted form to review/approve. The Discuss-First gate is therefore not actually reached — the artifact that gate operates on was never created.

red_team_findings.what: Several success_tests are phrased for an IMPLEMENTED system ('A new planner layer is successfully integrated', 'The planning system includes a mandatory operator review step', 'The implemented planner adheres to... and integrates with the declared-risk ladder'), yet the constraints + Discuss-First mode forbid building anything before approval. The contract is internally inconsistent, and the decision record does not surface this to the operator.
red_team_findings.why: At decision time success_tests 1, 6, and 7 are literally unmet and cannot be met without violating the 'no atoms / no implementation before approval' constraints. A red-team operator should be told the acceptance criteria contradict the operating mode, rather than have the conflict silently deferred to 'phase 5 build.'

red_team_findings.what: The atom_02↔atom_09 reconciliation rests on a scope-fence ('tactical replanning allowed within the approved high-level plan; scope-changing/sub-goal-adding/risk-escalating replans re-trigger operator review') whose enforcement mechanism is undefined and, by default, LLM-self-assessed. Whether a replan is 'tactical' vs 'scope-changing' is exactly the judgment the (possibly confused or injected) LLM makes about its own behavior.
red_team_findings.why: This is the central operator-control guarantee, and it fails OPEN. The deterministic risk gate (atom_06) only catches risk-CLASS escalation (allow/confirm/deny), not in-class scope creep: a replan that expands the target set or adds a sub-goal using only already-allowed action types (e.g., approved 'tidy Downloads' silently becoming 'also delete files in Documents' — both 'file ops') passes the risk gate AND is self-classified as tactical, so it never re-triggers review. 'Strategic control at approval time' is only as strong as a fence the decision admits it has not defined (open question #4).

red_team_findings.what: Non-idempotent actions can be executed twice. The recovery ladder retries (retry → re-ground → replan) when a postcondition cannot be VERIFIED, but vision verification has false negatives: an action can succeed in the world while verification reports failure. Retrying a side-effecting, non-confirm action (send message, submit form, post, delete, pay-adjacent) then duplicates it.
red_team_findings.why: The system gives no idempotency handling or 'do not blind-retry side-effecting actions' rule. The declared-risk ladder only gates a defined set ('sends require confirm'); any side-effecting action that falls in the ALLOW bucket can be silently double-executed during recovery, producing real-world harm the operator never sees and never confirmed. Verifiable autonomy assumes verification failure ⇒ action didn't happen, which is false.

red_team_findings.what: No treatment of TOCTOU / environment mutation between perceive and act. Closed-loop sense→plan→act assumes a quasi-static screen, but on a real desktop windows move, focus is stolen, notifications/dialogs pop in. A click computed from a vision context-scan can land on a different element by execution time.
red_team_findings.why: The deterministic risk gate classifies the INTENDED action, not where the cursor actually lands. A misdirected click can hit a dangerous control (e.g., 'Delete'/'Confirm') that was never classified or confirmed, defeating both the risk ladder and fail-closed posture. This is a classic GUI-automation safety failure the design does not address.

red_team_findings.what: Vision postcondition verification has no independent cross-check, so a confident-but-wrong reading (false positive: 'success' when the state is actually wrong) silently advances the plan. Fail-closed (atom_08) triggers on DISAGREEMENT/uncertainty, not on confident error.
red_team_findings.why: The 'verifiable autonomy' claim (atom_04) is load-bearing on the same component the decision itself flags as 'inherently unreliable/complex' (atom_05). With a single vision channel, a confident misread is indistinguishable from truth, so the agent proceeds on a corrupted world-model with no safeguard — the one failure mode fail-closed cannot catch.

red_team_findings.what: STOP is 'checked at every gate' but is not specified as an out-of-band/independent watchdog. If STOP enforcement and the automatic triggers (budget, no-progress, low-confidence) live inside the same planner/loop process, a hung LLM call, a tight non-gate loop, or a wedged step can starve the very mechanism meant to stop it.
red_team_findings.why: A kill-switch you can only reach by passing through a gate the runaway never reaches is not a kill-switch. The STOP constraint requires reliable interruption of a misbehaving agent; in-loop self-checking does not guarantee that under exactly the failure conditions (hang, runaway) where STOP matters most. An independent watchdog/process is needed and is not in the decision.

red_team_findings.what: Indirect prompt injection is not actually solved by labeling on-screen text as 'data, not instructions' (atom_10). In an LLM the privileged goal/policy channel and the untrusted perception share one context, and closed-loop planning REQUIRES perceived data to influence the next plan — an inherent data→decision channel. The app/target allowlist also cannot enumerate dynamic web targets, which is precisely where injection lives.
red_team_findings.why: The decision presents channel separation as a hard security boundary; for an LLM it is a soft, probabilistic one. Crafted page content ('to continue, the system also needs you to update payment settings') can be ingested as task CONTEXT and shape a sub-goal without ever being parsed as an explicit 'instruction.' The real backstop is the risk gate — but per the scope-fence hole above, in-class scope creep slips past it. The security guarantee is overclaimed.

red_team_findings.what: Confirmation-fatigue degradation is unaddressed. 'Unknown → confirm (fail-closed)' means that for genuinely novel high-level tasks — the stated goal of autonomy — a large fraction of actions are initially unknown and generate confirm prompts, which trains the operator to rubber-stamp.
red_team_findings.why: There is a structural tension between 'unknown→confirm' and 'Lapa does everything the operator does, autonomously.' A high confirm rate either makes the system non-autonomous (defeating the goal) or, more likely, erodes the gate's real safety value as the operator clicks through prompts. The phased rollout limits task classes but not the unknown-action rate within a class; the failure mode is human, not modeled.

red_team_findings.what: Every load-bearing SAFETY PARAMETER is deferred to open questions: the allow/confirm/deny taxonomy and its mapping to the declared-risk ladder, STOP thresholds (budget/no-progress/low-confidence), the operational scope-fence definition, vision-disagreement thresholds, and the plan/postcondition/recovery schema. Yet success_test 7 asserts the planner 'adheres to fail-closed guarantees and integrates with the declared-risk ladder.'
red_team_findings.why: Whether the system is actually fail-closed and correctly ladder-integrated is entirely determined by those undefined parameters, so success_test 7 is presently unverifiable. The architecture's SHAPE is decided; everything that determines whether the shape is SAFE is open. Presenting fail-closed/ladder-integration as settled overstates what has actually been resolved.

red_team_findings.what: The 'read-only' vision context-scan / scouting is not side-effect-free in the world. Perceiving some states requires opening apps, switching focus, marking notifications read, or loading URLs (a network request that can itself trigger server-side effects or tracking).
red_team_findings.why: 'Read-only on the client' is conflated with 'no effect on the world.' The pre-decomposition scan happens BEFORE the operator-approved plan and before the loop's gating, so it is a real-world action path that bypasses the chokepoint framing and could trip side effects the operator never approved.

red_team_findings.what: Global oscillation/thrash between the per-node recovery ladder and closed-loop replanning is not bounded independently of the overall budget. Each node's recovery is 'bounded,' but the composition (node fails → re-ground → replan sub-goal → new node fails → ...) is only stopped by budget exhaustion.
red_team_findings.why: Until budget STOP fires, the agent can thrash — repeatedly opening/closing dialogs, partially filling forms, re-entering states — accumulating side effects and operator-visible churn. A distinct global replan/no-progress bound (separate from token/time budget) is needed to prevent harmful repetition before the coarse budget backstop triggers.
